sentences: In a winter mountain washed entirely in pale grey ink stands a single red house.
And from across a bridge, a visitor dressed in blue is making his way towards it.
This is Winter Landscape, painted by Kim Su-cheol, who used the pen name Buksan, in the late Joseon period.
It is painted in colour on paper as a tall hanging scroll, 119 centimetres high and only 46 centimetres wide.
It belongs to the National Museum of Korea in Seoul, and it is also known by its Korean title, Donggyeong sansudo.
Look first at the lines of poetry written near the top.
They say, roughly, that the valley and the hills are silent and there is no one to ask the way, yet the visitor still finds the house of the recluse Lin Bu.
Thanks to this poem, we know exactly whose story the picture tells.
Lin Bu lived in China during the Song dynasty.
He is said to have made his home deep in the hills by the West Lake and not to have come down to the town for twenty years.
He spent his days with his cranes and his plum trees, and later generations admired him deeply.
So this is a plum-blossom studio painting, a hermit at home among the blossoms.
Now look at the mountains and rocks.
There is almost no shading at all; their shapes are set down with short outline strokes alone.
They are washed with light ink and finished with small moss dots that work almost like decoration.
This bold simplicity is the most distinctive feature of Kim Su-cheol's painting.
Now search for the house and the people in it.
In a picture made almost entirely of ink, only Lin Bu's house and Lin Bu's own robe are red.
The guest crossing the bridge to see him wears blue, so the two colours face each other brightly.
Kim Su-cheol was active in the middle of the nineteenth century, but the years of his birth and death are not known.
Because he was close to the middle-class painters and calligraphers of his day, scholars believe that he too came from that class.
He was especially good at landscapes and flowers.
In the summer of 1849 he took part in the contest at which Kim Jeong-hui judged his pupils' paintings.
That contest was held at the house of the painter Jeon Gi.
A letter also survives showing that Kim took commissions and sold paintings with Jeon Gi acting as his go-between, so we know the two men were close.
He was famous for quick, sketchy brushwork, yet he seems to have planned each picture first with an underdrawing in willow charcoal.
With his clear, transparent colours and daring omissions, he is regarded as a painter who brought a fresh sensibility to late Joseon art.
Step back and look again: grey mountains, a red house, a guest in blue.
Like the poem that says a friend's house can be found even with no one to ask the way, think of someone you would like to go and visit first this winter.
